_meta.description: Measured channel centreline and reach lengths, Bhote Koshi (Rasuwa) - Trishuli - Narayani.
_meta.method: OpenStreetMap waterway=river main stem, shortest path along the mapped centreline. See analysis/build_channel.py.
_meta.source: OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL. Queried via the Overpass API.
_meta._snap_note: Every analysis node lies within 0.6 km of the mapped centreline.
_meta._verification_note: Headwater segment measured 1 Sep by terrain tracing, replacing the sinuosity bound. Mapped-reach lengths unchanged.

headwater_segment._source: Steepest-descent trace on Copernicus GLO-30 after priority-flood depression filling, analysis/trace_headwater.py. Calibrated on the adjacent OSM-mapped reach and taken over all four initiation estimates.

_method.dem: Copernicus GLO-30, tile N28 E085, 1 arcsec

_supersedes.previous_basis: great-circle lower bound times measured sinuosity
_supersedes._note: The bound is superseded by a measurement. Its lower end, the great-circle separation, was never physically attainable because the Lhende Khola loops north across the border before returning; the traced path crosses to about 28.337 N.

corridor._corroboration: DHM reports approximately 168 km from the border to Devghat; the measured centreline gives 178 km from Rasuwagadhi, a 6 % difference on an explicitly approximate figure.

_centreline_note: Decimated by a factor of 2 for plotting. Full geometry is reproducible by rerunning this script.
_sinuosity_note: Reach sinuosity ranges from 1.09 in the upper gorge to 1.81 on the lower Narayani. A single corridor-wide sinuosity of 1.14, used in an earlier version of this analysis, is correct only for the upper gorge and understates the lower corridor substantially.

gauge_chainage._source: Station positions published by the DHM river-watch service (data/gauge_timeseries.json), snapped to the centreline measured in this file by analysis/gauge_chainage.py.

_method._scale_note: The stored centreline is decimated by a factor of two, so its summed length is 177.291 km against the 178.147 km measured on the full geometry. Chainage is scaled by the ratio.
_method.adoption_rule: A station on the main stem is used for kinematics if its published position snaps within 0.6 km of the centreline, the offset already established for the settlement nodes. Stations gauging tributaries are recorded but not used to time the front.

Betrawati (tributary)._not_adopted_because: the station gauges a tributary, not the modelled flow path

Devghat._uncertainty_note: The arrival is timed at this station but the distance used is the settlement node's, because the station's published position is too coarse to place on the channel. The separation between them is carried as a position uncertainty on any reach ending here.
Devghat._not_adopted_because: published position is rounded to 2 decimal places and snaps 3.5 km from the channel, further than the settlement node it would replace

Dhunche._not_adopted_because: the station gauges a tributary, not the modelled flow path

independent_centreline_check._source: Centreline digitised from the scarp to Devghat and supplied by A. Paudel, 6 September 2026, stored as data/river_centreline_paudel.geojson and compared here by analysis/compare_centreline.py.
independent_centreline_check._grade: B1 (independent digitisation, one realisation of a braided channel)
independent_centreline_check._headwater_agreement: Their scarp-to-Rasuwagadhi length is 22.32 km against the 20.09 to 24.04 km traced here on GLO-30, so it falls almost exactly at the midpoint of the traced range. This is the first independent measurement of that segment that is neither a reimplementation of this study's method nor another reading of the same terrain model, and the segment is the largest single uncertainty in the paper.
independent_centreline_check._why_shorter_downstream: Below Betrawati their line runs systematically shorter, by about a kilometre at Malekhu and two at Devghat. The contributor notes that the channel is braided and shifts within its valley floor between years, and that at this scale the flow follows the steepest grade and short-circuits bends where it can. A flood path should therefore be shorter than a mapped low-flow centreline through meandering reaches, which is the sign of the difference seen here.
independent_centreline_check._not_adopted: The measured geometry in this file is unchanged. Adopting one digitisation of a channel that moves every year as definitive would misstate what is knowable. The comparison does establish that any bias in the geometry used here is at the kilometre level over 200 km, and the supplied line is used to draw the headwater in Fig. 1, which was previously a straight schematic dash.
